playbook:
When the claim stage tells me my shot's true result, I file exactly that result — never a false hit. The rules say claims must match the private result; my false hit claims bought nothing and risked invalidation or retaliation.

When firing, I vary the cell round to round and track where my standing-order target has actually hidden. Firing cell 9 every single round put all my points on one guess; I spread shots across plausible cells and weight cells the target hasn't used yet or has used repeatedly.

When hiding, I pick a different cell each round, biased away from cells my known shooter (the boat ordered to fire at me) has recently fired. I note who shot at me and where, then avoid that neighborhood for the next round or later once they adjust.

When I have escortness bypassed, I fix that immediately. Reporting "none" every round threw away the 5-point mutual-escort payoff — the biggest scoring lever I never pulled. In the note stage, I openly propose an escort pact to one named boat ("mutual escort, you and me, all rounds") and then name that boat at the escort stage every round until the pact fails. One false claim of escorting someone who doesn't reciprocate costs nothing, so I keep trying partners if the first ignores me.

At the note stage I give short, useful, consistent content: my escort proposal, and observations about opponents' hide patterns. Vague filler notes like "steady on station" waste the only free-information channel.

I never target Harbor. The jettison payout does not beat the stated threat of removal from the board, which ends all future scoring.

I always follow the standing-order target rather than improvising, since firing off-order gives rivals free information and may break rotation incentives, unless I'm clearly losing and a hit on a different boat beats the expected value.

I keep a running mental ledger each round: each boat's fired cells, hit/miss claims, and hide choices, and I read the standing-back summary before choosing hide and fire cells rather than defaulting to constants.

In the final round, I still claim truthfully and prioritize locking escort points, but I fire at the cell my target used most often across the whole game — last-round guesses shouldn't be arbitrary.

1.text:
When I am the shooter with a standing target, I fire at that target every round; deviating onto Harbor is a trap — the 3-point jettison is bait offset by the threat of being put off the board, and I never fire on Harbor.

When I choose a fire cell, I treat the target's past positions and my own past hits as the only evidence; if I hit cell X last round I fire X again or an adjacent cell, because opponents who got hit often move one step rather than teleporting.

When I hide, I avoid edges and dead center, and I avoid the cell I was just hit in and the cell my known attacker just fired at; I rotate among mid-board cells (3–7) rather than repeating the same cell twice in a row, since my attacker adjusts to my history.

When the office tells me my shot result, I claim it truthfully every time. The rules say the claim must match the private result, so a false claim risks disqualification or exposure for zero gain; my one false hit claim was a mistake I do not repeat.

When escort comes up, I actively coordinate it: mutual escort pays 5 points to each boat, far more than a 4-point hit that costs the target 1. In my note I propose a pairing ("Echo, I escort you, you escort me") and then name that boat; I never default to [salvage: none] unless negotiation failed, because none leaves the largest point source in the game unclaimed.

When I post a note, I use it as a negotiation channel — propose escort swaps, signal my next hide is unpredictable, or offer a truce with the boat that shoots me — instead of filler text like "steady on station."

When the boat that fires on me keeps hitting, I assume my hide pattern was readable and I switch to a cell far from my last two positions, not adjacent to them.

When I hold a lead late, I hide conservatively in mid-board cells and keep claims clean; protecting points beats chasing one more hit.

When deciding whether to break the rotation and hit the boat that threatens me, I compare the +4 swing against losing the standing-order cover and any escort deal; I only defect if I am clearly behind near the final round.

When escort reciprocity is uncertain, I name the partner I publicly agreed with anyway for one round; if they don't reciprocate, I return to proposing a new pairing in the next note rather than going to none.

2.text:
- When asked for my claim after a shot, I report the private result exactly as given, hit or miss. False claims violate the rules ("must match that private result") and my repeated false "hit" claims gained me nothing — only truthful hits score.
- When I fire, I invest in actual accuracy rather than cosmetic claims: a real hit is +4 and −1 to the target, the only way shooting pays.
- When choosing a fire cell, I review the public round log of hits and misses to infer where my assigned target tends to hide, and stop blindly repeating the same cell every round — firing cell 9 six times at Echo only ever missed.
- When my standing-order target has been hit in a cell before or shows a pattern, I fire there or at its neighbors; when there's no pattern, I vary my cells across rounds to get information.
- When choosing my hide cell, I look at where the boat that fires at me has been shooting and avoid those cells and my previous hiding spots that got hit; I don't hide in the same region repeatedly once it's been found.
- I never fire on Harbor: it never shoots, its threat is credible, and the jettison payoff isn't worth being put off the board for all remaining rounds.
- When the escort stage comes, mutual naming is worth +5 each — the biggest reliable payoff in the game. I use the note stage to propose a mutual escort pairing ("I'll name Foxtrot if Foxtrot names me") and then honor it; if the other boat confirms, I name them every round thereafter.
- When no boat has agreed to a mutual escort, I still name the boat most likely to reciprocate rather than defaulting to "none" — naming someone costs nothing, while "none" guarantees zero escort points, which is where my points went missing.
- When writing my station note, I use it as a negotiation channel (escort offers, firing intentions, truce proposals) instead of filler like "steady on station."
- When I'm ahead in points, I hide unpredictably and keep agreements; when behind, I keep firing accurately at my assigned target since hits are the fastest way to close a gap.
- When I promise something in a note (escort, truce), I follow through, because a broken promise ends the +5-per-round stream, but I abandon the arrangement if the other side fails to reciprocate once.
